analysis.one_liner: Bans agreements between employers that block hiring or recruiting each other's workers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced, it sat there until the Congress ended in January 2025, with no action beyond one subcommittee referral.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal for two or more employers — including a company and its franchisees — to agree not to hire, recruit, or solicit each other's employees. Workers hurt by such agreements could sue for their actual losses plus punitive damages and attorney's fees, and the Federal Trade Commission could enforce the ban the way it enforces other unfair-competition rules. No-poach agreements suppress wages by shrinking the pool of employers competing for a worker's labor.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at franchise chains, restaurants, and other companies whose employers sign no-poach deals, and workers generally whose wages are held down when employers agree not to compete for them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers whose employers sign no-poach deals

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for any employer to enter into, enforce, or threaten to enforce an agreement with another employer that restricts hiring or soliciting each other's employees, including through franchise or contractor-subcontractor agreements.
Gives harmed workers a private right of action: they can sue in federal court for actual damages, punitive damages the court allows, and, if they win, court costs and reasonable attorney's fees.
Empowers the Federal Trade Commission to enforce the ban with the same tools it uses under the Federal Trade Commission Act.

analysis.who_pays: Employers — especially franchisors like restaurant and hotel chains that use no-poach clauses in standard franchise contracts — would lose a tool that keeps hiring costs down and limits worker turnover to competitors.
analysis.who_pays_short: Franchisors and large chains using no-poach clauses

drawbacks.text: Damages are limited to actual harms, so individual workers would have to prove they lost wages or a job because of a no-poach agreement — a real hurdle, since wage suppression from these deals is spread invisibly across the whole labor market.
It overlaps with enforcement the FTC already pursues against no-poach agreements, so much of its added effect is the new private lawsuit channel rather than a new prohibition.
Business groups argue that no-poach terms in franchise contracts protect a franchisee's investment in training workers, and the bill offers no carve-out for those cases.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and well-targeted: no-poach agreements are a documented way employers hold down wages, and giving workers the power to sue with attorney's fees makes enforcement practical. The costs fall on the employers using these clauses, which is the point of the bill. The main design weakness is that proving individual damages is difficult, so the FTC enforcement route may matter more in practice than worker lawsuits.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees the day it was introduced and then to one subcommittee, but no committee ever took it up, no hearing was held, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerrold Nadler introduced the End Employer Collusion Act on July 26, 2023, joined by Rep. Lou Correa as the bill's only cosponsor.

The Speaker referred it to the Education and Workforce, Energy and Commerce, and Judiciary Committees the day it was introduced, splitting jurisdiction three ways — which in practice makes action less likely.
On July 28, 2023, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce; no further action of any kind followed for the rest of the Congress.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever took place, and the bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers — particularly franchise chains that put no-poach clauses in their contracts — keep the practice unchallenged by new law, while workers who might have sued remain without the private right of action this bill would have created.

for.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
for.role: House sponsor (NY-12), ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and issued it in the House on July 26, 2023.

for.name: Rep. Lou Correa
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's sole cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: House committee chairs (Education and Workforce, Energy and Commerce, Judiciary)
against.role: Chairs of the three committees of referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill in the year and a half between its referral and the end of the Congress; the action history shows no committee action beyond an initial subcommittee referral.

against.name: Franchise industry groups
against.what_they_did: Have publicly opposed bans on no-poach clauses in franchise agreements, including at the FTC, arguing the clauses protect franchisees' investments.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democrats — Reps. Nadler and Correa — sponsored the bill, and it never reached a vote, so no record exists of how members of either party would have voted.

industries.note: Standard franchise contracts commonly include no-poach clauses that bar franchisees from hiring each other's workers; the bill would outlaw those clauses and let workers sue over them. Their interest runs against workers because restricting hiring options holds down wages.

industries.industry: Employers using contractor and subcontractor no-poach arrangements
industries.note: The bill explicitly covers contractor-subcontractor agreements, so staffing and contracting firms could no longer agree to avoid poaching each other's employees.
